btos.label: Mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction (NAICS 21)

name: Mining
blurb: Autonomous haulage and ore-body modelling in the sector that automated early, from USGS exploration data and Earth MRI to Rio Tinto, Komatsu, KoBold, and the AI-native explorers.

points.desc: Census BTOS reports mining-sector AI use directly from firms.
points.name: Adoption is measured, not guessed

points.desc: The Mineral Resources Program is the public record of US mineral assessments - the satellite, geophysical, and historical data that exploration models train on.
points.name: USGS anchors the exploration data layer

points.desc: The USGS Earth Mapping Resources Initiative is systematically re-mapping US geology with modern geophysics - the dataset behind machine-learning prospectivity work on critical minerals.
points.name: Earth MRI maps the country for critical minerals

points.desc: The company's own automation program - autonomous haul trucks and drills operating at scale - is the primary-source record of what day-to-day operational AI looks like in production mining.
points.name: Rio Tinto runs the operations proof point

points.desc: One of the two dominant mining-equipment makers publishes its autonomous haulage and fleet-management technology - where operational AI ships as machinery.
points.name: Komatsu documents the autonomous equipment layer

points.desc: The National Mining Association tracks regulatory change and technology adoption across American mining operations - the sector's US policy layer.
points.name: NMA is the US trade association

points.desc: The International Council on Mining and Metals tracks ESG standards, automated safety monitoring, and digital transformation across the major international operators.
points.name: ICMM sets the global operator standards

points.desc: The Society for Mining, Metallurgy & Exploration publishes the working-group research on AI, machine learning, and automation in mineral processing.
points.name: SME carries the technical research

points.desc: The AI-first exploration company applies machine learning and geospatial modelling to target battery-metal deposits - lithium, cobalt, copper, nickel - and is the sector's clearest AI-native bet.
points.name: KoBold Metals is the AI-native explorer

points.desc: The US copper major applies machine-learning models to processing - maximizing mill throughput and ore recovery at existing operations rather than finding new ones.
points.name: Freeport-McMoRan optimizes the mill with ML

points.desc: The major gold miners use AI for drill-core analysis, predictive maintenance, and automated safety monitoring - Newmont's and Barrick's own technology pages are the record.
points.name: Barrick and Newmont apply AI to gold

points.desc: Computer-vision core scanning (GeologicAI) and real-time ore characterization at the mine face (Plotlogic) - the specialist vendors turning geology into a machine-readable input.
points.name: GeologicAI and Plotlogic scan the rock itself

summary: Autonomous haulage and ore-body modelling are the established deployments in a sector that adopted automation early. Mining AI splits into two horizons: exploration - long-term forecasting from satellite, magnetic, and core-scan data toward drilling targets - and site operations, where sensor streams and telemetry drive machinery, maintenance, and safety minute by minute.

analysis.body:
AI adoption in mining remains measured but growing. According to the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, 8.2% of firms in mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction reported using AI in the last two weeks as of the latest survey period, up from 7.2% in the prior period. This direct measurement from operating firms provides the baseline: adoption exists but remains concentrated among larger operators and specialized vendors rather than representing widespread deployment across the sector.

The application of AI in mining divides into three distinct layers. At the exploration stage, the USGS Mineral Resources Program and its Earth Mapping Resources Initiative provide the foundational data layer—modernizing mapping of the nation's subsurface geology through geochemical and geophysical surveys that machine-learning prospectivity models train on. At the mineral-characterization stage, specialist vendors like GeologicAI apply computer vision and multi-sensor core scanning (RGB, XRF, hyperspectral, and LiDAR) to turn drill core and ore face into machine-readable datasets, reducing logging inconsistency and freeing geologists to interpret results rather than catalog samples. KoBold Metals exemplifies the AI-native explorer, applying machine learning and geospatial modeling to target battery metals like copper and cobalt.

Operational AI concentrates in autonomous equipment and mill optimization. Komatsu, one of the two dominant mining-equipment makers, has entered strategic partnership with AIM Intelligent Machines to deploy autonomous operation of bulldozers and hydraulic excavators, embedding the technology directly into machinery. Rio Tinto operates autonomous haul trucks and drills at scale, representing the primary production proof point for day-to-day operational AI. Freeport-McMoRan applies machine-learning models to mill processing to maximize throughput and ore recovery at existing operations, while major gold producers like Newmont use AI for drill-core analysis, predictive maintenance, and automated safety monitoring.

Vendor concentration and capital deployment reflect the capital intensity of mining. Equipment makers like Komatsu and established operators like Rio Tinto, Barrick, Newmont, and Freeport-McMoRan dominate deployment, while specialist vendors (GeologicAI, KoBold, Plotlogic) focus on data capture and interpretation layers rather than end-to-end systems. The National Mining Association serves as the sector's policy voice before Congress and federal agencies, while the International Council on Mining and Metals tracks ESG standards, safety automation, and digital transformation across major international operators, indicating that regulatory posture centers on safety, emissions, and responsible resource management rather than AI governance per se.

Organizations evaluating AI deployment in mining should recognize that the sector's AI layer is mature in autonomous equipment and mill optimization, where ROI evidence exists in production at scale, but remains specialized in exploration and geophysics. The integration of USGS Earth MRI data with machine-learning models represents a structural opportunity for prospectivity improvement, but requires both domain expertise in geology and access to proprietary historical drilling and assay data. The Society for Mining, Metallurgy & Exploration carries the technical research that translates these developments for engineering professionals. Adoption barriers appear less technical than organizational—concentration among major operators suggests deployment requires capital scale, long operational horizons, and existing IT infrastructure—and regulatory posture remains focused on the safety and environmental outcomes AI enables rather than on the technology itself.
